Males are more likely to harbor a greater diversity of pathogens compared to females due to their increased propensity to disperse, exposing them to encounter more pathogens (Streicker et al., 2016). Also, host systems that are sexually dimorphic in immunity and infection outcomes can provide the pathogen with two selectively distinct environments (Gipson and Hall, 2016; Khan and Prasad, 2011), imposing far-reaching impacts on disease transmission, especially in populations with skewed sex ratios. Life-history traits such as lifespan, sexual maturity, and reproductive output that make certain species ideal for natural reservoirs (Han et al., 2016) can perhaps be mediated via resource allocation trade-offs (Schwenke et al., 2016), where limiting the activation of costly immune responses might promote other fitness traits and favor pathogen tolerance. For example, several host species like rodents that thrive in human-dominated landscapes usually have a fast pace of life, reducing investment in immunity and thereby harboring more pathogens at any given timepoint (Gibb et al., 2020) – early maturity and high early-reproductive output (e.g., increased reproduction at a young age; see Medzhitov et al., 2012) can trade-off with immune responses allowing rodents to become competent natural reservoirs for zoonotic pathogens (Ostfeld et al., 2014). In nature, frequently encountered stressful environments such as poor nutrition can also have severe impacts on immune investment and pathogen tolerance (Wang et al., 2016). For example, burying beetle (Nicrophorus vespilloides) feeding on a low protein diet showed increased tolerance to Photorhabdus luminescens (Miller and Cotter, 2018). Another study on Cuban tree frog (Osteopilus septentrionalis), however, found increased tolerance to skin penetrating nematode Aplectana sp. when maintained on proteinaceous insect diets (Knutie et al., 2017), suggesting that impacts of nutrition on tolerance are perhaps host- and pathogen-specific. Nonetheless, considering these multifaceted implications of host physiology and various life-history traits in immunity and disease tolerance, it is imperative to analyze the role of these parameters in explaining pathogen prevalence data collected during disease surveillance. Different life-history traits can interact closely to drive the level of and pathogen prevalence. For instance, in addition to dispersal (discussed above; Streicker et al., 2016), higher pathogen burden in males can be explained by their lower investment in immunity as they typically experience stronger intra-sexual competition and a greater variance in reproductive success (Bateman, 1948; Zuk and Stoehr, 2002). As implicated above, even age, sexual maturity, pace-of-life, or nutritional status might manifest their effects on immunity and tolerance by altering reproductive investments. Sexually dimorphic immune investment, causing sex-specific divergence in tolerance and pathogen prevalence, may evolve as a function of intersexual resource competition (Li and Kokko, 2019) or mating strategies (Bagchi et al., 2021) We certainly need future studies to explore these intimate interactions and pinpoint complex life-history and physiological features of reservoirs that can be attributed to their disease-carrying ability.

### Suggestion 3: identify the host-pathogen coevolutionary dynamics to predict emerging infections

Analyzing changes in genes involved in host-pathogen interactions can generate crucial insights about their association over an evolutionary timescale (Woolhouse et al., 2002). For instance, virulence genes involved in continuous host-pathogen arms race tend to display positive selection (dN/dS > 1) in the codons that are involved in the interaction sites between the virus and host cell receptor (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011). Indeed, host cell receptors for viruses like HIV (cluster of differentiation 4), filovirus (Niemann-Pick C1), and several coronaviruses (angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 ) have been shown to undergone positive selection across different mammalian orders (Pontremoli et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020). SIV envelope protein binding domain of CD4 receptor (D1 domain) in many African primate species has undergone diversification in the coding sequence (Zhang et al., 2008). The amino acid replacements in the D1 domain can prevent viral envelope glycoprotein (Env)-CD4-mediated cell entry in multiple African primate species, protecting them from SIV infection (Zhang et al., 2008). A recent study has further revealed that diversification of CD4 receptor, with as many as 11 coding variants in Moustached monkey Cercopithecus cephus, might be under balancing selection as an outcome of the long-term coevolutionary arms-race with primate lentiviruses (Russell et al., 2021). Quantifying selection pressures acting at various host receptor-pathogen interfaces by calculating respective dN/dS ratios (Yang and Bielawski, 2000) can thus help us in unearthing evidence of the evolutionary history of exposure; for example, (1) high or low degree of filovirus exposure to natural reservoir bat vs. novel human hosts respectively; or (2) genomic signatures left by pathogenic primate lentiviruses in susceptible primate species vs. other long-term SIV-infected species such as sooty mangabeys evolving specific mechanisms to avoid the disease progression (Russell et al., 2021). The consequences of long-term positive selection on pathogens might also transcend into evolved variants with new antigenic properties and possible expansion of the host range (Bedi et al., 2013). Indeed, in the case of SARS outbreak in 2002, selection on the spike gene of SARS-CoV was positively correlated with its spillover from palm civets to humans (Chinese SARS Molecular Epidemiology Consortium, 2004). The binding affinity of the virus spike protein towards human ACE2 changed from low to high due to mutations in two critical amino acids, turning it into a pandemic strain (Chinese SARS Molecular Epidemiology Consortium, 2004).

Levels of pathogen sequence divergence can accelerate more with increased polymorphism of host receptors (Gupta et al., 2009; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011; Warren et al., 2019), allowing pathogens to infect and adapt to another host more effectively (Daugherty and Malik, 2012). For instance, a recent study that analyzed ACE2 receptors in Chinese horseshoe bats (Rhinolophus sinicus) found multiple such highly polymorphic sites in the receptor regions, which interacts with the spike proteins of a coronavirus isolated from the same species of bats named as SARSr-CoV (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus isolated from R. sinicus; Guo et al., 2020). As expected, binding affinities of SARSr-CoV to these polymorphic receptors varied widely, making some cells more susceptible to viral entry than others. However, the most interesting aspect of their study was that, when tested upon human cell lines, some of these SARSr-CoV strains even showed higher binding affinity to human ACE2 compared to that of R. sinicus, hinting at their potential to cause spillover in overlapping human populations (Guo et al., 2020). Given the direct implications of these results in spillover and human health, we suggest the need for more such analyses to uncover the coevolutionary outcomes of pathogens from the diverse host interface (e.g., reservoirs vs. other host species), both at the spatial as well as the temporal scales.

Future studies can also test whether and how coevolving viral pathogens can maintain genetic polymorphism for adaptation to the host immune environment. Probing signatures of coevolution in accessory proteins that target host-associated restriction factors can aid understanding of the complex interplay between immune defense and viral adaptations. Indeed, the importance of such evolutionary processes has been implicated in previous studies where modified strains of HIV (simian tropic HIV-1 strain; stHIV-1) rapidly evolved to antagonize host restriction factor tetherin by acquiring mutations in the accessory protein Vpu within merely four passages through an atypical HIV-1 host species pigtailed macaques (Maccaca nemestrina; Hatziioannou et al., 2014). There are several other accessory genes as well such as Nef, Vif, and Vpr that have evolved in lentiviruses to counteract host antiviral immune responses (Sauter and Kirchhoff, 2018). Hence, in addition to finding links between host immune strategies (resistance vs. tolerance), life-history, and pathogen prevalence, revealing coevolutionary dynamics and resulting genetic diversification of circulating pathogens (i.e., key molecules involved in host entry, infectivity. and virulence) can greatly advance our understanding of their range expansion via spillover.

### Suggestion 4: set up controlled proof-of-principle laboratory coevolution studies to test hypotheses generated in the wild and provide mechanistic insights

It is important to note that due to the involvement of a multitude of factors ranging from genetics to environmental variations influencing animal populations, evaluating disease tolerance and pathogen spillover can be complicated in the wild. Data from field experiments can certainly provide information about larger patterns and processes such as heterogeneity in immune responses and genetic diversity in circulating pathogen strains, but creating a controlled empirical paradigm is perhaps necessary to generate more mechanistic insights into the actual micro-evolutionary processes. Finding greater pathogen diversity and prevalence in reservoir hosts with lower inflammatory responses, reduced rate of fitness loss, and increased polymorphism in pathogen receptor sites might indicate a potential correlation between coevolution, tolerance, and diverse zoonotic pathogen pool, but the causal link is still difficult to establish. Using common garden experimental setups that allow rearing and maintenance of well-characterized focal organisms under study in their semi-natural environmental conditions (e.g., large field enclosures for wild mice) can help us to partially overcome the uncertainties associated with quantifying parasite burden and estimating fitness traits in the wild (Barrett et al., 2019; Klemme et al., 2020).

Yet it might be challenging to answer some of the most fundamental questions, such as do hosts actually evolve tolerance to their natural pathogens? If so, how do we track such evolutionary processes? Besides gathering clues from comparative studies using various host populations, laboratory experimental evolution using tractable animal models (with known biology and genomic information) can be an excellent alternative to test these possibilities (Khan et al., 2017b; Masri et al., 2013; Prasad and Joshi, 2003). They can enable us to directly track host-pathogen dynamics and test diverse hypotheses on the evolution of host tolerance, genetic diversifications of pathogens, and spillover risk to overlapping susceptible host populations. Owing to rapid generation time and easy maintenance, insect hosts, in particular, provide an excellent system to conduct such long-term evolution experiments (e.g., see Ford et al., 2020; Khan et al., 2017b; Mukherjee et al., 2019; but also see Kohl et al., 2016 for study in voles). While in principle any well-characterized insect model, with known biology and genetic information, can be used to test these basic hypotheses, mosquito hosts can be particularly useful both for the fundamental discovery as well as their direct relevance to human health (Huang et al., 2019). For example, filarial infections that exert strong selection pressure in mosquito hosts by inducing high mortality can be a valuable resource to test whether fitness costs are minimized by evolving tolerance (Aliota et al., 2010; Bartholomay, 2014). Experimental evolution studies can also be combined with a comparative dataset where multiple wild-caught mosquito populations are analyzed to quantify the natural variation in tolerance to filarial worms, followed by probing their underlying immune profiles. Subsequently, populations showing lower tolerance can be identified and subjected to repeated exposure to filarial infection across generations to test whether the level of tolerance can be further increased by modulating inflammatory responses. Such an integrated empirical framework might help in establishing the proposed causal link between coevolutionary history and pathogen tolerance (see Figure 4).

![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/68874/elife-68874-fig4-v1.jpg)

**Figure 4.:** Susceptible host populations can be exposed to the coevolving pathogens at every generation and assayed periodically to estimate the changes in the tolerance level.

A similar experimental paradigm can also be used to test whether shared evolutionary history is responsible for tolerance in the vector hosts against their natural pathogens. For example, mosquito species Armigeres subalbatus is a natural vector for the zoonotic filarial worm Brugia pahangi whom they can tolerate, but not the morphologically and biologically similar pathogen Brugia malayi (Aliota et al., 2010; Aliota et al., 2007), which is perhaps not as prevalent as B. pahangi in the mosquito hosts (Muslim et al., 2013). In fact, mosquito hosts resist B. malayi infection using costly immune responses (Aliota et al., 2010; Aliota et al., 2007). Can long-term coevolution reverse such effects of B. malayi infection? By experimentally imposing long-term selection with the new pathogen B. malayi, we can verify the causal connection between the length of coevolutionary history and the level of host tolerance and parasite evolution. Subsequently, genetic analyses can uncover the mechanistic basis of adaptive changes in host immunity (e.g., possible modulation of costly inflammatory responses; Märkle et al., 2021) and pathogen replication and transmission potential (Siva-Jothy and Vale, 2021).

Laboratory evolution studies can also be implemented to track the evolutionary origin of established molecular mechanisms underlying tolerance strategies adopted by vector hosts. For example, both A. albopictus and A. aegypti can rapidly synthesize viral-derived DNA (vDNA), which is crucial for their tolerance and survival against chikungunya virus and dengue virus, respectively (Goic et al., 2016). How did such mechanisms evolve? A possible empirical framework is to (1) collect naturally isolated Aedes populations lacking (or with inherently lower) viral tolerance; (2) impose long-term viral selection to directly test whether stronger tolerance is correlated with increased vDNA synthesis; and (3) finally, test whether such evolved tolerance can be reversed by reducing vDNA synthesis (using reverse genetics) to verify its functional role (see Goic et al., 2016). Since previous experiments already demonstrated the role of tolerance in increasing the transmission intensity and vectorial capacity in mosquitoes (Dharmarajan et al., 2019), experiments showing direct evolution of parasite tolerance and infectivity in important vectors will make crucial contributions to public health (Lambrechts and Saleh, 2019).

## Conclusion and further implications for public health

In closing, as disease-causing pathogens from wild animals are emerging at an unprecedented rate across the globe, we must acknowledge that our understanding of specific ecological interactions and adaptive features of reservoir hosts is still at a nascent stage. A few theoretical models and experiments have provided broader insights into specific immune strategies to cater persistence of zoonotic pathogens (Alexander et al., 2012; Brook et al., 2020; White et al., 2018), but their oversimplistic assumptions might have limited inferential value in nature. To fill this gap, we have compiled a range of direct and indirect evidence of tolerance that can potentially explain the pathogen prevalence across host-pathogen systems, indicating its wider relevance to disease spread and spillover. However, despite the conceptual appeal, predictions based on the tolerance of reservoir hosts in catalyzing emerging infections still lack empirical rigor. There are no experiments that have thoroughly verified the whole process; that is, evolution of pathogen tolerance in reservoir animals to spillover. Recent analyses appear promising as they reveal the genetic basis differentiating the pathogen resistance from tolerance in critical human diseases such as HIV, where a high viral load often coincides with minimal disease progression as a feature of tolerance (Regoes et al., 2014). Also, there are experiments with bacteriophages that have confirmed that genetic variations are indeed required for viral emergence and host expansion (Dennehy et al., 2010). Still, targeted studies in natural reservoirs are needed to jointly probe the whole spectrum of tolerance to pathogen emergence, validating their cascading impacts on the spillover.

To this end, an integrated immune-centric understanding of naturally occurring variable infection outcomes across different host-pathogen systems and their specific ecological contexts, life-history, and evolutionary implications can be crucial. Systematic verification of the proposed links between pathogen prevalence, pathogen diversity, and host tolerance across a range of ecological contexts is needed, followed by deeper evolutionary insights into the maintenance of latent pathogen reservoirs and conditions that trigger spillover events. We believe that a hypothesis-driven experimental framework based on previous theoretical models is timely and will conceptually motivate a wide range of biologists to adopt a proactive disease surveillance program complemented with deeper ecological, evolutionary, and immunological thinking. Finally, we expect that our review will not only be relevant to the present crisis created by pandemic and emerging infections, but it will also provide a newer understanding of other important aspects of public health research such as infectious disease control (e.g., consequences of disease tolerance via vaccination) and the dynamics of noninfectious diseases (e.g., increased risk autoimmune disorders in geographical regions where improved hygiene has reduced pathogen burden; Bach, 2018).

claims.source: Finally, sooty mangabeys and African green monkeys, natural hosts of SIV, also remain healthy and do not develop AIDS (Chahroudi et al., 2012; Wetzel et al., 2017) possibly because of their long coevolutionary history with lentiviruses (dating back to 5–6 million years; Compton and Emerman, 2013), which enables them to prevent the deleterious consequences of SIV infections (Rudensey et al., 1995).

claims.claim: Successful spillover to novel host warrants multiple sequential steps including pathogen release, survival, infection, and spread.
claims.source: Successful spillover to novel host warrants multiple sequential steps (Plowright et al., 2017). Briefly, pathogens should first be released by their reservoir hosts either directly into the environment or a new host through different plausible transmission routes such as consumption, animal bites, or sexual interactions (Webster et al., 2017). Pathogens should then survive until it encounters novel susceptible hosts whom it might infect directly or by undertaking a further round of adaptation to the new host environment (Parrish et al., 2008). Finally, once the pathogen establishes infection in the novel host by evading the immune responses, it then needs to spread effectively in the population (Plowright et al., 2015; Subudhi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research describing the spillover process.

claims.claim: The duration of the host's infectivity, population density, and size might dictate the success of consecutive steps in spillover transmission chain.
claims.source: At each step of this transmission chain, the duration of the host's infectivity, population density, and size might dictate the success of the consecutive step (Remien and Nuismer, 2020; Wolfe et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: An important precondition for spillover can be the maintenance of a sufficiently large and diverse zoonotic pathogen pool with the potential to overcome the species barrier.
claims.source: However, before all these fine-scale micro-evolutionary downstream processes can begin, potentially an important precondition can be the maintenance of a sufficiently large (Mollentze and Streicker, 2020) and diverse (Remien and Nuismer, 2020) zoonotic pathogen pool with the potential to overcome the species barrier.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The role of reduced inflammation and disease tolerance in maintaining persistent zoonotic pathogen populations in reservoir species has been implicated.
claims.source: Also, the role of reduced inflammation and disease tolerance in maintaining such persistent zoonotic pathogen populations in reservoir species has already been implicated (Pavlovich et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2019), but how it can boost transmission and spillover is relatively unclear.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.source: For example, both infectious period and transmission potential can increase if the host tolerates the pathogenic infection by evolving an efficient repair mechanism to counter the damages caused by the pathogen and immune responses (Henschen and Adelman, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the context that zoonotic pathogens cause severe disease in humans but often produce no disease in their natural reservoir hosts, highlighting a fundamental asymmetry in infection outcomes across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-established observations in the field of zoonotic disease research, supported by general scientific consensus and presented as foundational knowledge. These claims accurately describe the current understanding of zoonotic disease patterns.

results.result: The authors propose that long-term co-evolution enables reservoir hosts to evolve tolerance to zoonotic pathogens, which increases pathogen circulation and creates genetically diverse pathogen pools that may facilitate spillover events.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C4 are speculative hypotheses about evolutionary mechanisms. While conceptually plausible and central to the manuscript's thesis, these claims lack direct experimental validation and are presented as proposed mechanisms rather than demonstrated facts. The manuscript itself acknowledges this gap in empirical evidence (C34).

results.result: Phylogenetic relatedness and spatial proximity between hosts increase the risk of pathogen sharing and spillover, as exemplified by primates harboring diverse human pathogens and synanthropic species sharing more zoonotic pathogens with humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C11 are well-supported by multiple citations to previous research. The examples of primate pathogens (Plasmodium knowlesi, SIV/HIV) and synanthropic species are documented in the literature and provide concrete evidence for the role of phylogenetic relatedness and spatial proximity in zoonotic transmission.

results.result: Mathematical models and recent analyses indicate that the number of zoonotic viruses with spillover risk increases proportionally with both the total number and genetic diversity of viruses in reservoir animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C13 are supported by citations to recent mathematical models and analyses. These claims represent established theoretical predictions in the field, though the manuscript notes that direct causal links remain to be demonstrated experimentally.

results.result: Reservoir species can maintain long-term infections and persistently shed pathogens into their environment, as demonstrated by Egyptian fruit bats with Marburg virus, water buffalo with Brucella abortus, and cattle with pathogenic E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by citations to experimental and observational studies. These examples provide concrete evidence of persistent infection and pathogen shedding in reservoir hosts, supporting the manuscript's argument about the role of tolerance in maintaining pathogen circulation.

results.result: Bats and rodents are efficient reservoir hosts that harbor over 60% of known zoonotic pathogens and can asymptomatically carry diverse human pathogens due to dampened innate immune pathways that allow stable viral infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are well-supported by multiple citations to previous research and review articles. The characterization of bats and rodents as major reservoir hosts with dampened immunity is consistent with current scientific understanding and supported by empirical evidence.

results.result: Disease symptoms can result from immune overreactivity rather than ineffective responses, as exemplified by cytokine storms in HIV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 infections that cause immunopathological damage to host tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 are supported by multiple citations to previous research and WHO data. The concept of immunopathology and cytokine storms is well-established in the literature, and the SARS-CoV-2 example provides timely evidence of this phenomenon with documented mortality data.

results.result: The manuscript argues that traditional research has focused on resistance mechanisms while neglecting tolerance mechanisms, which allow hosts to coexist with pathogens by mitigating fitness costs without reducing pathogen burden, potentially explaining pathogen persistence and transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 accurately describe the historical bias in the field and define the concept of tolerance as distinct from resistance. These claims are supported by citations to foundational work on tolerance and acknowledge the gap in empirical research (C34), providing an honest assessment of the current state of knowledge.

results.result: Optimal immune strategies depend on ecological and life-history contexts and may shift between resistance and tolerance based on pathogenicity, infection frequency, and the balance between pathogen control and immunopathological costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 present a conceptual framework for understanding immune strategy evolution. While C36, C37, C38, and C42 are supported by citations, C39-C41 are explicitly speculative hypotheses about immune strategy switching. The manuscript acknowledges the lack of experimental evidence for these dynamic changes, making the overall result uncertain.

results.result: Multiple examples from natural populations demonstrate tolerance in the wild, including mourning doves with West Nile virus, Hawai'i 'Amakihis with avian malaria, field voles with parasites, and amphibian tadpoles with trematodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by citations to previous research on natural populations. These examples provide empirical evidence for tolerance in diverse taxa and ecological contexts, though the manuscript notes that exact mechanisms and evolutionary processes remain unclear.

results.result: Fruit bats exhibit molecular adaptations for tolerance including lack of pro-inflammatory gene induction, expanded type I IFN genes, modified NK cell receptors, and absence of inflammasome-activating genes, enabling them to tolerate viral infections while avoiding immunopathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are supported by multiple citations to molecular and genomic studies of bat immunity. The evidence for dampened inflammatory responses and their proposed coevolution with flight metabolism provides a mechanistic explanation for bat tolerance to viruses.

results.result: Sooty mangabeys and African green monkeys infected with SIV use anti-inflammatory cytokines (TGF-β and IL-10) to rapidly control acute inflammation and maintain CD4+ T cell proliferation, avoiding chronic immune activation and disease progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by multiple citations to previous research on SIV-infected primates. These findings provide mechanistic insights into how natural hosts control inflammation while maintaining immune homeostasis during persistent viral infection.

results.result: Rodents infected with hantaviruses and other pathogens maintain regulatory T cell responses and upregulate anti-inflammatory factors (TGF-β, FoxP3) to suppress inflammation and facilitate viral persistence while preventing immunopathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by citations to previous research on rodent immune responses to viral infections. The evidence for Treg-mediated immunomodulation provides a mechanistic parallel to the findings in primates and bats.

results.result: Mosquito vectors tolerate arboviral infections through tissue repair mechanisms (ISC proliferation to maintain midgut homeostasis) and upregulation of antioxidant pathways to counter oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by citations to previous research on mosquito-virus interactions. These examples extend the concept of tolerance beyond mammalian hosts to arthropod vectors, demonstrating the broader applicability of tolerance mechanisms.

results.result: The manuscript synthesizes evidence that reservoir hosts and vectors have repeatedly evolved either lower inflammatory responses or compensatory mechanisms to mitigate inflammation, enabling them to maintain balanced immunity and tolerate circulating pathogens without severe disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C66 and C67 represent reasonable inferences drawn from the multiple examples presented in the preceding sections (C48-C65). The synthesis is logical and consistent with the cited evidence, though it represents an interpretive conclusion rather than direct experimental demonstration.

results.result: A longitudinal study of wild Soay sheep demonstrated that tolerance to intestinal worms is under strong positive directional selection, with tolerant individuals showing higher lifetime reproductive success and most variation explained by environmental rather than genetic factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are based on data from a well-designed longitudinal field study and supported by citations to theoretical models. This represents one of the strongest pieces of empirical evidence for the evolution of tolerance in natural populations, though it is limited to a single host-pathogen system.

results.result: Resistance and tolerance strategies differ in their evolutionary dynamics: resistance typically leads to host-pathogen arms races and may be maintained under stabilizing or balancing selection, while tolerance is predicted to evolve under directional selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by citations to theoretical and empirical research on the evolution of immune strategies. The contrast between resistance and tolerance provides important context for understanding why tolerance might be favored in reservoir hosts.

results.result: Comparative studies show that populations with longer coevolutionary history with pathogens exhibit higher tolerance, as demonstrated by house finches exposed to M. gallisepticum and Asian tiger mosquitoes exposed to heartworm.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by citations to experimental and comparative studies. These examples provide evidence linking coevolutionary history to tolerance evolution, with mechanistic support from cytokine expression data in house finches.

results.result: Phylogenetic analyses reveal that hantaviruses co-speciated with rodent subfamilies and lentiviruses have a 5-6 million year coevolutionary history with African primates, explaining the persistence and asymptomatic state of these viruses in their natural hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by citations to phylogenetic studies. These examples provide evolutionary context for understanding how long-term host-pathogen associations may lead to tolerance, though direct causal links between coevolutionary history and tolerance mechanisms remain to be experimentally validated.

results.result: Land-use changes and deforestation create spatial overlap between wildlife, livestock, and humans, increasing spillover risk, as exemplified by Chinese workers dying from Histoplasma infection in Guyana.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C82 are supported by citations to previous research and a specific case report. The Histoplasma example illustrates the consequences of human encroachment into natural ecosystems, though the manuscript acknowledges uncertainty about whether coevolutionary history would have altered the outcome.

results.result: Successful spillover requires multiple sequential steps (pathogen release, survival, infection, spread), with the maintenance of large and diverse pathogen pools in reservoir hosts serving as an important precondition, potentially facilitated by tolerance mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by citations to previous research on spillover processes. The manuscript appropriately notes that while large pathogen populations have been predicted to serve as sources of zoonotic diseases, direct causal links between tolerance and spillover remain unclear (C87).

results.result: Tolerance mechanisms may enhance spillover risk by extending infectious periods through tissue repair, selecting for less virulent pathogens in reservoir hosts, increasing pathogen circulation and shedding, and raising overall disease burden in host populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 present a logical chain of reasoning supported by citations to previous research and theoretical models. However, the connections between tolerance, pathogen dynamics, and spillover risk remain largely theoretical. While individual components are supported (e.g., C94 on bat populations), the complete causal pathway from tolerance to enhanced spillover has not been experimentally demonstrated.

results.result: Spillover is a rare event that depends not only on pathogen abundance but also on genetic diversity of the pathogen pool, which can enhance prospects for jumping species barriers by harboring useful mutations for establishing infection in new hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by citations to previous research on spillover dynamics and pathogen evolution. The emphasis on genetic diversity as a factor in spillover risk is well-grounded in evolutionary theory and empirical observations.

results.result: Extended infectious periods and relaxed selection in tolerant hosts provide opportunities for pathogen evolution through mutation and genetic exchange, particularly in multi-segmented genome viruses like influenza that can undergo reassortment.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by citations to experimental evolution studies and research on viral recombination. The bacteriophage φ6 example (C100) provides direct experimental evidence for host range expansion under competitive conditions, supporting the broader hypothesis.

results.result: Recombination between viral lineages can produce variants with enhanced transmission potential, as demonstrated by SIVcpz (which contributed to HIV-1 pandemic) and SARS-CoV-2 variants, with immunocompromised hosts potentially serving as sites for viral evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by citations to phylogenetic analyses and recent research on SARS-CoV-2 evolution. The examples provide evidence for viral recombination and evolution in hosts with altered immune responses, though direct links to tolerance mechanisms remain speculative.

results.result: Genetic exchanges between diverse pathogen groups are possible in natural conditions, as evidenced by recombinant viruses found in tolerant hosts (sooty mangabeys, mosquitoes, bats), with possibilities increasing proportionally with time spent together inside a tolerant host.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C115 present intriguing examples of potential inter-viral recombination (C110-C113) and documented recombination in bat coronaviruses (C111, C115). However, the evidence for recombination between highly divergent viral groups is limited and mechanisms are unclear (acknowledged in C110). The inference that tolerance increases recombination opportunities (C114) is logical but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Pathogens can rapidly evolve immune evasion mechanisms, as demonstrated by SIV variants that escape cytotoxic T cells and downregulate host receptors, and SARS-CoV-2 variants with reduced vaccine neutralization, though some functions may be lost during evolution to new hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are supported by citations to previous research on viral evolution and immune evasion. The examples demonstrate pathogen adaptation to host immunity, though the relationship to tolerance mechanisms is not directly established.

results.result: Long-term tolerogenic host-pathogen interactions may lead to loss of pathogen immune evasion mechanisms, as seen with Myxoma virus in Australia, though this outcome is not universal, as SIV retains infectivity across species after long-term association.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by citations to previous research, with the Myxoma virus example providing concrete evidence for virulence attenuation. However, C121 is speculative, and the contrasting SIV example (C125) demonstrates that outcomes are pathogen-specific, limiting generalizability.

results.result: Leaky vaccines that reduce disease symptoms without preventing infection create tolerance-like conditions that can lead to evolution of more virulent pathogen strains and vaccine escape variants, as demonstrated in poultry with Marek's disease virus, PRRSV in pigs, and IBV in chickens.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C132 are supported by multiple citations to vaccination studies in agricultural animals. These examples provide important parallels to natural tolerance and demonstrate how tolerance-like conditions can influence pathogen evolution, though the mechanisms may differ from natural tolerance.

results.result: In the wild, immune responses may operate at suboptimal levels due to resource constraints and physiological states, with host ecology, life-history, and physiological constraints serving as important mediators of immune strategies and infection outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C133 and C134 are supported by citations to previous research and represent a growing consensus in the field. These claims provide important context for understanding why laboratory studies may not fully capture immune dynamics in natural populations.

results.result: Rodents and bats harbor 60% and 30% of known zoonotic viruses respectively and commonly utilize landscapes occupied by humans and domestic animals, increasing opportunities for pathogen exchange at multiple species interaction interfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C135 and C136 are supported by citations to previous research. These claims establish the public health relevance of studying these taxa and provide context for the manuscript's focus on understanding tolerance in reservoir hosts.

results.result: The PREDICT surveillance program generated valuable knowledge on mammalian pathogens and aided pandemic response, but spillover events are inherently stochastic, and there is doubt about the direct ability of such programs to prevent pandemics, necessitating continued funding for monitoring at-risk human populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C142 are supported by citations and present a balanced assessment of surveillance programs. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges both the contributions and limitations of programs like PREDICT, providing a nuanced perspective on pandemic preparedness strategies.

results.result: Deforestation and biodiversity loss are major drivers of zoonotic disease risk, with South Asia having lost approximately 30% of forest land and potentially serving as a hotspot for emerging infectious diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 are supported by multiple citations to previous research on land-use change and disease emergence. The specific data on South Asian deforestation provides concrete evidence for the scale of habitat alteration in a region of high spillover risk.

results.result: Life-history traits influence pathogen prevalence through multiple mechanisms: males harbor more pathogens due to dispersal and immune trade-offs, sexual dimorphism creates distinct selective environments for pathogens, and fast-paced life histories in rodents reduce immune investment.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C149 are supported by citations to previous research on life-history and immunity. These claims provide important context for understanding variation in pathogen prevalence across individuals and populations, though the manuscript notes that effects are complex and context-dependent (Table 1).

results.result: Nutritional status affects tolerance in complex and potentially contradictory ways, with burying beetles showing increased tolerance on low-protein diets but Cuban tree frogs showing increased tolerance on high-protein diets.
results.evaluation: Claims C150 and C151 are supported by citations to previous research but demonstrate contradictory effects of nutrition on tolerance. The manuscript appropriately presents these as examples of host- and pathogen-specific effects, highlighting the complexity of tolerance mechanisms.

results.result: Host-pathogen coevolution leaves genomic signatures of positive selection at virus-receptor interfaces, with host cell receptors for HIV, filoviruses, and coronaviruses showing positive selection across mammalian orders, and CD4 receptor diversification in African primates potentially under balancing selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 are supported by citations to phylogenetic and molecular evolution studies. The evidence for positive selection at host-pathogen interfaces provides molecular support for long-term coevolutionary dynamics, though the functional consequences for tolerance are not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Positive selection on the SARS-CoV spike gene during the 2002 outbreak was correlated with spillover from palm civets to humans, with mutations in two critical amino acids increasing binding affinity to human ACE2 and creating a pandemic strain.
results.evaluation: Claims C157 and C158 are supported by citations to molecular epidemiology studies of the SARS outbreak. This example provides direct evidence for the role of positive selection in facilitating spillover and adaptation to new hosts.

results.result: Polymorphism in host receptors can accelerate pathogen sequence divergence, as demonstrated by highly polymorphic ACE2 receptors in Chinese horseshoe bats that show variable binding to SARSr-CoV, with some viral strains showing higher affinity for human ACE2 than bat ACE2.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C162 are supported by citations to recent research on bat ACE2 receptors. The finding that some bat coronavirus strains bind human ACE2 more strongly than bat ACE2 (C162) provides direct evidence for spillover potential and highlights the importance of studying receptor polymorphism.

results.result: Experimental evolution studies demonstrate rapid viral adaptation to new hosts, with modified HIV strains evolving to antagonize host restriction factors within four passages through pigtailed macaques, and multiple lentiviral accessory genes having evolved to counteract host antiviral responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C163 and C164 are supported by citations to experimental studies. The rapid evolution of HIV in an atypical host (C163) provides direct experimental evidence for the potential of viruses to adapt to new host immune environments.

results.result: Mosquito-filarial worm systems provide opportunities to study tolerance evolution, with Armigeres subalbatus tolerating Brugia pahangi but resisting the similar pathogen Brugia malayi through costly immune responses, potentially reflecting differences in coevolutionary history.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 are supported by citations to previous research on mosquito-filarial interactions. This system is proposed as a valuable model for testing hypotheses about tolerance evolution, though the causal link to coevolutionary history remains to be experimentally validated.

results.result: Mosquitoes can rapidly synthesize viral-derived DNA (vDNA), which is crucial for their tolerance and survival against chikungunya and dengue viruses.
results.evaluation: Claim C168 is supported by a citation to previous research on mosquito antiviral mechanisms. This represents a specific molecular mechanism underlying tolerance in arthropod vectors.

results.result: Recent analyses reveal genetic basis for differentiating resistance from tolerance in HIV, and bacteriophage experiments confirm that genetic variation is required for viral emergence and host expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C169 and C170 are supported by citations to recent analyses and experimental studies. These examples provide evidence for the genetic basis of tolerance and the role of genetic variation in host range expansion, supporting the manuscript's broader arguments.
